newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: ECONOMIC FEATURE - APEC a turning point for Philippines.
newsitem.headline: ECONOMIC FEATURE - APEC a turning point for Philippines.

text.p: This month's Asia-Pacific summit will mark a turning point for both its Filipino hosts and for the 18-member grouping itself, analysts and organisers say.
For the Philippines it's like a grand coming out party, celebrating what many economists regard as a remarkable economic revival after decades of abysmal failure.

For the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, it is time for concrete results to emerge from the "vision" of what is potentially the world's biggest and wealthiest free trade area -- accounting for something like half of all world productivity.
"The time for visioning is finished," Jesus Estanislao, one of President Fidel Ramos's top advisers on APEC, said.

"What we need to do in Manila is get on into the field of action, to concrete and specific steps every economy will take ... in order to realise the vision that was first adopted in Seattle and further concretised in Bogor and Osaka," he said, referring to the three previous APEC summits.
U.S. President Bill Clinton, China's Jiang Zemin and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto will join Ramos and other APEC leaders at their summit on November 25 in Subic, north of Manila.
Critics dismiss the summit as one big photo opportunity and some diplomats and officials privately agree, with the real work completed weeks before by senior officials and ministers.

All year, members have been drafting, refining and revising an Individual Action Plan (IAP) detailing how they will reach APEC's goals of lowering all trade an investment barriers in the region by 2010 for developed members and 2020 for the less well off.
For example, the Philippines has set an interim target for 2004, by when it pledges to drop tariffs on imports to a 3-10 percent range. Some of its tariffs currently stand at 50 percent.

Overall, the commitments made in these IAPs go slightly further than APEC members' obligations under the World Trade Organisation and its predecessor, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), officials say.
"APEC is supposed to be better than (GATT), so that it can show the WTO what can be achieved," Philippine Trade and Industry Secretary Cesar Bautista said.

Apart from approving the IAPs, the leaders are also expected to agree on a U.S. proposal to form a united front at next month's WTO meeting in Singapore on pushing for tariff-free trade in information technology products such as computer hardware.
Officials say the summit will also endorse proposals on sharing expertise and technologies among APEC members and on environmental protection and promoting small enterprises.

"APEC cannot just be about trade and investment alone but also about human develoment and respectful of proper environmental standards," Estanislao, a former finance minister and now president of Manila's University of Asia and the Pacific, said.
The leaders, however, are likely to staunchly resist any efforts to move APEC away from its consensual, voluntary approach to the formal, legally-binding methods of, for example, the European Union.
"That's not the Asian way. Our preference in Asia is let's talk, you'll have to take my word," Estanislao said.
"What we are trying to do is build a community in the Asia-Pacific region. We're not trying to build a 'Fortress Asia-Pacific' as what we think is happening in Europe."
The Subic summit will also differ from previous meetings in the much higher profile accorded the private sector, a personal project of President Ramos.

Some 400 business executives will meet with the leaders in Manila on November 24 and APEC is expected to formally adopt private sector recommendations, such as a programme to help tackle the region's massive infrastructure needs.
The event is a major triumph for Ramos himself, who has masterminded his nation's economic revival by precisely the kind of free market policies APEC espouses.
"The timing of the summit is considered very fortuitous for the Philippines," said University of the Philippines political science professor Alex Magno.
"We've shown very good macroeconomic figures the last two years and in a way the APEC provides us with an opportunity to have a coming out party," he said.
It is also a chance for the Philippines to finally shed its image as a land of great charm but little else other than political turmoil, natural disasters and plain incompetence.
There has long been a perception "that the Filipino can never do anything right ... that the only thing they can organise is a fiesta and a siesta", Estanislao said.
"But some real substance will come out of Manila and Subic so, we are shedding the image that the Philippines is a do-nothing economy and that all we can do is bungle things."
